topic.name: Equations of Ellipses Centered at the Origin

question.text: What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation $\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1?$
question.explanation:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by \[ \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1. \]

In the given equation, we have $a^2=16$ and $b^2=9.$

  • Since $a^2 = 16,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a = \sqrt{16}=4.$

  • Since $b^2 = 9,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b = \sqrt{9} = 3.$

So the semi-major axis has length $a=4,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=3.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a = 2 \cdot 4 = 8,$ and the minor axis has length $2b= 2 \cdot 3 =6.$

question.text: What is the equation of the ellipse given above?
question.explanation:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by \[ \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1. \]

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=5$ and the vertical radius has length $b=7.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is \[ \begin{align*} \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} &= 1 \\[3pt] \dfrac{x^2}{5^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{7^2} &= 1 \\[3pt] \dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{49} &= 1. \end{align*} \]

example.title: Determining the Equation of a Tall Ellipse

question.text: What is the equation of the ellipse given above?
question.explanation:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by \[ \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1. \]

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=5$ and the vertical radius has length $b=\dfrac{17}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is \begin{align*} \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2} &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{x^2}{5^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{\left(\dfrac{17}{2}\right)^2} &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{\left(\dfrac{289}{4}\right)} &= 1 \\[5pt] \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{4y^2}{289}} &= 1. \end{align*}
